title: Asclepias speciosa

{{Short description|Species of flowering plant}} {{Use mdy dates|date=July 2021}} {{Speciesbox |image = Asclepias speciosa1jakesmome.jpg |genus = Asclepias |species = speciosa |authority = [[John Torrey|Torr.]] | status = {{TNCStatus}} | status_system = TNC }} [[File:Asclepias speciosa.jpg|thumb|''Asclepias speciosa'', West Eugene wetlands, Oregon]] '''''Asclepias speciosa''''' is a milky-sapped [[perennial plant]] in the dogbane family ([[Apocynaceae]]), known commonly as the '''showy milkweed''' and is found in the western half of North America.(1) {{cite web|first=Michelle|last=Stevens|date=May 30, 2006|url=https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/cs_assp.pdf|title=Plant guide for ''Asclepias speciosa''|location=Washington, D.C.|publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]: [[Natural Resources Conservation Service]]|access-date=July 12, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210712172322/https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/cs_assp.pdf|archive-date=July 12, 2021|url-status=live}}
(2) {{cite web|last1=Young-Mathews|first1=A.|last2= Eldredge|first2=E.|year=2012|url=https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/orpmcfs11338.pdf|title=Plant fact sheet for showy milkweed (Asclepias speciosa)|publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]: [[Natural Resources Conservation Service]], Corvallis Plant Materials Center, Oregon, and Great Basin Plant Materials Center, [[Fallon, Nevada]]|access-date=July 12, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210401052315/https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/orpmcfs11338.pdf|archive-date=April 1, 2021|url-status=dead}}
(3) {{cite web|url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/forb/ascspe/all.html|title=Asclepias speciosa|location=Washington, D.C.|publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]: [[United States Forest Service]]|access-date=July 12, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210307062424/https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/forb/ascspe/all.html|archive-date=March 7, 2021|url-status=live}}{{cite book|first=Karen|last=Wiese|year=2000|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/sierranevadawild00wies/page/50/mode/2up?q=Asclepias+speciosa|chapter=Showy Milkweed: ''Asclepias speciosa''|url=https://archive.org/details/sierranevadawild00wies/page/n1/mode/2up|title=Sierra Nevada wildflowers: a field guide to common wildflowers and shrubs of the Sierra Nevada, including Yosemite, Sequoia, and Kings Canyon National Parks|page=50|isbn=0585362831|oclc=47011272|lccn=00022385|location=[[Helena, Montana]]|publisher=Falcon Publishing, Inc.|via=[[Internet Archive]]|access-date=July 12, 2021}} ==Description== This flowering plant is a hairy, erect [[perennial]] growing up to {{Convert|120|cm|abbr=on}} in height.{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/348/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |pages=348 |orig-date=1979}} The pointed, elongate, simple, entire [[leaves]] are about {{Convert|10-20|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long and arranged oppositely on stalks. Milky sap is released when the leaves or stems are bruised or cut.{{Cite web |title=Asclepias speciosa - Plant Finder |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=276791 |access-date=2022-02-16 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}} The flowers are about {{Convert|2|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} wide, hirsute, pale pink to pinkish-purple, and occur in dense umbellate [[cymes]]. Their corollas are reflexed and the central flower parts, five hoods with prominent hooks, form a star shape. The fruit is a rough [[Follicle (fruit)|follicle]] about {{Convert|5-10|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and filled with many flat oval seeds, each with silky hairs. This species flowers from May through August. Many other species in the genus ''[[Asclepias]]'' are toxic, particularly to livestock.{{Cite book |last=Fagan |first=Damian |title=Wildflowers of Oregon: A Field Guide to Over 400 Wildflowers, Trees, and Shrubs of the Coast, Cascades, and High Desert |publisher=[[FalconGuides]] |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-4930-3633-2 |location=Guilford, CT |pages=187 |oclc=1073035766}} == Distribution and habitat == This species is native to the western half of North America,{{cite web |title=Asclepias speciosa Torr.: showy milkweed |url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=ASSP |access-date=July 12, 2021 |publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]: [[Natural Resources Conservation Service]] |location=Washington, D.C.}} including [[British Columbia]] and from the [[Cascade Range]] in [[California]] east to the [[central United States]]. It grows along streams, dry slopes, open woodland areas, and roadsides. == Ecology == ''Asclepias speciosa'' is a specific [[monarch butterfly]] food and [[habitat]] plant. Additionally, phenylacetaldehyde produced by the plants attracts ''[[Synanthedon myopaeformis]],'' the red-belted clearwing moth.{{Cite journal |last1=Eby |first1=Chelsea |last2=Gardiner |first2=Mark G.T. |last3=Gries |first3=Regine |last4=Judd |first4=Gary J.R. |last5=Khaskin |first5=Grigori |last6=Gries |first6=Gerhard |date=2013-04-01 |title=Phenylacetaldehyde attracts male and female apple clearwing moths, Synanthedon myopaeformis, to inflorescences of showy milkweed, Asclepias speciosa |journal=Entomologia Experimentalis et Applicata |language=en |volume=147 |issue=1 |pages=82–92 |doi=10.1111/eea.12045 |bibcode=2013EEApp.147...82E |issn=1570-7458 |s2cid=84552298}} It is also a larval host for the [[dogbane tiger moth]] and the [[queen butterfly]].The Xerces Society (2016), ''Gardening for Butterflies: How You Can Attract and Protect Beautiful, Beneficial Insects'', Timber Press. [[Monarch Watch]] provides information on rearing monarchs and their host plants.{{cite web |title=Monarch Watch |url=http://www.monarchwatch.org/index.html |access-date=September 27, 2015 |work=monarchwatch.org}} Efforts to restore falling monarch butterfly populations by establishing [[Butterfly gardening|butterfly garden]]s and monarch migratory "waystations" require particular attention to the target species' food preferences and population cycles, as well to the conditions needed to propagate and maintain their food plants.(1) {{cite web |last1=Borders |first1=Brianna |last2=Lee–Mäder |first2=Eric |year=2014 |title=Milkweed Propagation and Seed Production |url=https://www.fws.gov/southwest/es/Documents/R2ES/Pollinators/8-Milkweeds_Handbook_XerSoc_June2014.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210704050023/https://www.fws.gov/southwest/es/Documents/R2ES/Pollinators/8-Milkweeds_Handbook_XerSoc_June2014.pdf |archive-date=July 4, 2021 |access-date=July 12, 2021 |work=Milkweeds: A Conservation Practitioner's Guide: Plant Ecology, Seed Production Methods, and Habitat Restoration Opportunities |publisher=[[Xerces Society|The Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation]] |location=[[Portland, Oregon]] |pages=21–95}}
(2) {{cite journal |last1=Landis |first1=Thomas D. |last2=Dumroese |first2=R. Kasten |year=2015 |title=Propagating Native Milkweeds for Restoring Monarch Butterfly Habitat |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/rm/pubs_journals/2015/rmrs_2015_landis_t001.pdf |url-status=live |journal=International Plant Propagators' Society, Combined Proceedings (2014) |volume=64 |pages=299–307 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308083021/https://www.fs.fed.us/rm/pubs_journals/2015/rmrs_2015_landis_t001.pdf |archive-date=March 8, 2021 |access-date=July 11, 2021 |via=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]: [[United States Forest Service]]}} For example, where it grows in Michigan and surrounding areas and in the [[western US]], monarchs reproduce on ''A. speciosa'', especially when its foliage is soft and fresh. Because monarch reproduction in those areas peaks in late summer when milkweed foliage is old and tough, ''A. speciosa'' needs to be mowed or cut back in June or July to assure that it will be regrowing rapidly when monarch reproduction reaches its peak.{{cite book |author=National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine |url=http://www.trb.org/Publications/Blurbs/180186.aspx |title=Evaluating the Suitability of Roadway Corridors for Use by Monarch Butterflies |publisher=[[National Academies Press]] |year=2020 |isbn=9780309481328 |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=79–80 |doi=10.17226/25693 |lccn=2020935714 |oclc=1229163481 |id=[[National Cooperative Highway Research Program|National Cooperative Highway Research Program (NCHRP)]] Research Report 942 |quote='''''Could roadside mowing stimulate milkweed growth and support monarch breeding?''''' Limited research in eastern North America has shown that spring or summer mowing can promote new growth and extend the availability of milkweed plants for monarch breeding. Mowing may stimulate growth of some milkweed species, particularly those that spread through rhizomes like common milkweed (''A. syriaca'') and showy milkweed (''A. speciosa''). Summer (June or July) mowing in Michigan resulted in more monarch eggs on regenerated stems than unmowed stems. Summer (July) mowing and burning can increase green antelopehorn milkweed (''A. viridis'') availability in the late summer and early fall in the Southern Great Plains, whereas in areas without mowing, the milkweed has [[senescence|senesced]] by August. In the West, showy milkweed will regrow after summer mowing and continue to support monarch breeding (Stephanie McKnight, personal observation). However, more research is needed in other areas to determine the optimal timing and frequency of mowing that promotes not only milkweed but also nectar plants. It is also unknown if the benefit of additional milkweed availability in the fall outweighs the costs of the larval mortality caused by summer mowing. The benefits are likely greater in areas that primarily have breeding monarchs in the spring and fall and where the dominant species of milkweed spread by rhizomes. ''Sources: Alcock et al. 2016; Baum and Mueller, 2015; Bhowick 1994; Haan and Landis 2019; Fischer et al. 2015'' |author-link=National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine |bibcode=2020nap..book25693N |access-date=July 8, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200729123529/http://www.trb.org/Publications/Blurbs/180186.aspx |archive-date=July 29, 2020 |url-status=live |s2cid=218854539}} The seeds of some milkweeds need periods of cold treatment ([[Stratification (seeds)#Cold stratification|cold stratification]]) before they will germinate.(1) {{cite web |last1=Borders |first1=Brianna |last2=Lee–Mäder |first2=Eric |year=2014 |title=Milkweed Propagation and Seed Production: Stratification |url=https://www.fws.gov/southwest/es/Documents/R2ES/Pollinators/8-Milkweeds_Handbook_XerSoc_June2014.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210704050023/https://www.fws.gov/southwest/es/Documents/R2ES/Pollinators/8-Milkweeds_Handbook_XerSoc_June2014.pdf |archive-date=July 4, 2021 |access-date=July 12, 2021 |work=Milkweeds: A Conservation Practitioner's Guide: Plant Ecology, Seed Production Methods, and Habitat Restoration Opportunities |publisher=[[Xerces Society|The Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation]] |location=[[Portland, Oregon]] |pages=28–29}}
(2) {{cite journal |last1=Landis |first1=Thomas D. |last2=Dumroese |first2=R. Kasten |year=2015 |title=Propagating Native Milkweeds for Restoring Monarch Butterfly Habitat |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/rm/pubs_journals/2015/rmrs_2015_landis_t001.pdf |url-status=live |journal=International Plant Propagators' Society, Combined Proceedings (2014) |volume=64 |page=302 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308083021/https://www.fs.fed.us/rm/pubs_journals/2015/rmrs_2015_landis_t001.pdf |archive-date=March 8, 2021 |access-date=July 11, 2021 |quote=Many sources of milkweed seeds require stratification (cold, moist treatment) before sowing. In a review of stratification requirements for common milkweed, recommendations varied from as short as 7 days to as long as 11 months at 5°C (41°F) (Luna and Dumroese, 2013). Butterfly milkweed (A. tuberosa) germination increased from 29 to 48 to 62% as stratification duration increased from 0 to 30 to 60 days, respectively (Bir, 1986). Our informal natural stratification trial with showy (milkweed) and narrow leaf milkweed (A. fascicularis) in southern Oregon revealed that seeds began to germinate after 15 weeks in stratification (Fig. 3A). |via=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]: [[United States Forest Service]]}}
(3) {{cite news |last=Higgins |first=Adrian |date=27 May 2015 |title=7 milkweed varieties and where to find them |work=Home & Garden |publisher=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/home/a-world-of-milkweeds/2015/05/26/43fba7d6-fe6c-11e4-833c-a2de05b6b2a4_story.html |url-status=live |access-date=17 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926092547/https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/home/a-world-of-milkweeds/2015/05/26/43fba7d6-fe6c-11e4-833c-a2de05b6b2a4_story.html |archive-date=26 September 2020 |quote=Seed may be stubborn to germinate and may need a period of cold treatment.}}. To protect seeds from washing away during heavy rains and from seed–eating birds, one can cover the seeds with a light fabric or with an {{convert|0.5|in|mm|0|abbr=on|order=flip}} layer of [[Mulch#Straw mulch / field hay / salt hay|straw mulch]].(1) {{cite book |last1=Mader |first1=Eric |url=https://archive.org/details/attractingnative0000unse/page/113/mode/1up |title=Attracting Native Pollinators: Protecting North America's Bees and Butterflies: The Xerces Society guide |last2=Shepherd |first2=Mathew |last3=Vaughan |first3=Mace |last4=Black |first4=Scott Hoffman |last5=LeBuhn |first5=Gretchen |publisher=[[Workman Publishing Company#Imprints and distribution|Storey Publishing]] |year=2011 |isbn=9781603427470 |location=[[North Adams, Massachusetts]] |pages=113–114 |lccn=2010043054 |oclc=776997073 |access-date=July 7, 2021 |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}
(2) {{cite journal |last1=Landis |first1=Thomas D. |last2=Dumroese |first2=R. Kasten |year=2015 |title=Propagating Native Milkweeds for Restoring Monarch Butterfly Habitat |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/rm/pubs_journals/2015/rmrs_2015_landis_t001.pdf |url-status=live |journal=International Plant Propagators' Society, Combined Proceedings (2014) |volume=64 |page=302 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308083021/https://www.fs.fed.us/rm/pubs_journals/2015/rmrs_2015_landis_t001.pdf |archive-date=March 8, 2021 |access-date=July 11, 2021 |quote=Any of the standard seed propagation methods (Landis et al., 1999) are effective with milkweed. Direct sowing of non-stratified seeds during the fall followed by exposure to ambient winter conditions can be effective, but the seeds must be mulched and protected. Cover sown seeds with a thin mulch; research has found that common milkweed seeds germinated better when planted 1 to 2 cm (0.4 to 0.8 in.) deep than when at the soil surface (Jeffery and Robison, 1971). |via=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]: [[United States Forest Service]]}} However, [[mulch]] acts as an [[Thermal insulation|insulator]]. Thicker layers of mulch can prevent seeds from germinating if they prevent soil temperatures from rising enough when winter ends. Further, few [[seedling]]s can push through a thick layer of mulch.{{cite book |last1=Bush-Brown |first1=James |url=https://archive.org/details/americasgardenbo00bush/page/n2/mode/1up |title=America's garden book |last2=Bush-Brown |first2=Louise |publisher=[[Charles Scribner's Sons]] |year=1958 |location=New York |page=[https://archive.org/details/americasgardenbo00bush_0/page/768/mode/1up 768] |chapter=Chapter 32: Mulches |lccn=58005738 |oclc=597041748 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/americasgardenbo00bush_0/page/767/mode/1up |url-access=registration |via=[[Internet Archive]]}} == Uses == Native Americans used fiber in the stems for rope, basketry, and nets. Some Native Americans used the milky sap for medicinal purposes. Although care is needed to distinguish the species from highly toxic species in the genus, the young leaves and seed pods of ''A. speciosa'' can be boiled and eaten.{{cite book |last=Lyons |first=C. P. |author-link=C. P. Lyons |title=Trees, Shrubs and Flowers to Know in Washington |date=1956 |publisher=J. M.
